newsitem.title: USA: Cook Inlet lease sale draws only two bids.
newsitem.headline: Cook Inlet lease sale draws only two bids.

text.p: A controversial oil and gas lease sale for offshore tracts in Alaska's Cook Inlet drew only two bids Wednesday, both from Miami-based Forcenergy.

The federal lease sale, conducted by the U.S. Minerals Management Service, offered 101 blocks covering 427,800 acres in federal waters of the lower part of the inlet. Forcenergy's bids, for tracts near the community of Anchor Point, totaled $253,967, according to preliminary results released Wednesday.
Forcenergy is a recent entry into Cook Inlet and is expanding exploration there.

Bob Goll, MMS director for Alaska, said the agency had anticipated only a few oil company bids to be made in Cook Inlet Sale 149, which was vigorously opposed by environmentalists, fishermen, tourism operators and the area's Alaska Natives.
"This was really within what we had expected," Goll said after he read the bids in a ceremony Wednesday. "We were expecting only a handful."
The lease sale was severely reduced from an original planning area of 3.7 million acres, a response to concerns about conflicts between oil and gas development and fishing, recreation and tourism.
Many development supporters believed the sale area was reduced too much, Goll said, and that may have dampened industry interest.
Others argued that the lease sale should have been cancelled entirely, he said.
Among those opposing the sale was Alaska Gov. Tony Knowles, a Democrat.
Goll said the MMS plans to continue its negotiations with fishing groups, Natives and others to help mitigate any adverse impacts from possible oil development, he said.
"We will work closely with them to ensure that any operations are, if they occur in Cook Inlet, safe, and that space-use allocations are minimized," he said.
But Dorothy Childers of the Alaska Marine Conservation Council said such further negotiations are likely to be fruitless.
"The industry is expected to somehow work it out with the local people, and that's just not feasible," Childers said.
She said she was gratified that the lease sale drew only two bids -- a reflection, she said, of past dry holes drilled in the area rather than a desire by industry to avoid controversy.
"I think the interest is low, and that's good for fish," she said.

But she criticized the federal government for planning another lower Cook Inlet lease sale for 1999, despite longstanding local opposition to oil development there. The proposed sale area is the same that was orginially proposed for Sale 149, she said.
"It almost feels like the Minerals Management Service wants to exhaust the public," she said.

Cook Inlet, a swift-running channel that runs from Anchorage to the Gulf of Alaska, is well-used by commercial salmon and sport fishermen. It is also one of the state's most popular sites for recreation and tourism activities.
The northern part of the inlet is also the site of the state's oldest producing oil and gas fields.
